Primitives

Eyebrow

The small-caps label above a thing. It is the one recipe this system repeated most, and until now it had no home: twenty-eight CSS blocks combined text-transform: uppercase with --of-type-tracking-wide, and ten of them were in apps/site — ten page stylesheets that had each independently re-derived the same five declarations. A twenty-ninth was this generator's own chrome, which is why the card you are reading had an .eyebrow class before the library had the component.

Rarity Apparatus

Two tones, and it shipped with three. ink-muted and full ink, in that order above. The difference between them is how loudly the label competes with what it labels, not a palette choice — which is why they are named for their loudness rather than exposed as a colour prop. A colour prop would put a raw value back in a page, and check:tokens would fail the build; correct, but a slow way to learn it.

The third tone was ink-faint, it was the default, and removing it is the point. The survey counted three inks across the twenty-eight blocks and this component reproduced all three — but color.ink.faint is the LARGE-text ink, held to 3:1 rather than 4.5:1 on purpose, and an eyebrow is type.size.micro by definition. Most of the surveyed blocks were already below AA, so making the majority the default turned a defect repeated in ten page stylesheets into one every caller inherited. check:faint-ink named this file first. A tone no caller may correctly pass is a trap rather than an option, so it is gone from the union rather than merely demoted — and gone is what the gate cannot enforce by itself, since it matches a colour and a size in the same rule and a data-tone rule carries no size.

The element varies and the style does not, so as exists. The same recipe appears on a <dt> in a definition list, on a heading above an apparatus block, and on a plain <span> beside a year. Forcing one element would make the primitive unusable in two of those three; an eyebrow rendered as a <span> where a <dt> belongs breaks the list for a screen reader. The union is closed at six — a seventh should be somebody's decision, not a default.

No margin, and that is the load-bearing omission. Every surveyed block set its own distance to the thing below it, and those distances differed: a filter label sits closer to its control than a section kicker sits to its section. Spacing is a property of the relationship, not of the label, so it stays with the caller. A margin-block-end here would be wrong in most places it landed and would be overridden in a page stylesheet — which is the duplication this primitive exists to remove.

The migration was two call sites, not ten, and that is measured. Twenty-eight blocks share the five-declaration recipe; only three consist of the recipe and nothing else, and one of those is this component's own stylesheet. The other twenty-six each add something — font-weight in twelve of them, split three ways between medium, bold and regular, which is why weight is deliberately absent here — or a whole layout. Absorbing those would mean growing props for weight, spacing and display until this was a styling API rather than a primitive, which is the restyle that "compose, never restyle" is aimed at. The value from here is in what gets written next.

What it deliberately does not absorb. Table headers in the printings and syntax tables keep their semantics from <th>. The wordmark is size-base at full ink and is not a label above anything. And the labels inside BrassSeal, FactChip, Pagination, ResultRow, SearchField and StatePill stay theirs — reaching into a sibling primitive to restyle its innards is the coupling this library exists to avoid. That duplication is deliberate; a shared type treatment is not a shared component.
